title: The Welfare State
hook: Should the state guarantee a floor below which no one can fall? The welfare state is modern government's answer — and one of its biggest, most-debated commitments.
key_points: The welfare state is government provision for citizens' basic economic security and well-being.
Typical pillars: pensions, healthcare, unemployment support, and education.
It aims to cushion people against risks like illness, old age, and joblessness.
Debates center on its size, cost, and effects on the economy and individual responsibility.
content_html: One of the defining features of modern government is the welfare state: the set of programs through which the state takes responsibility for the basic economic security and well-being of its citizens. Its premise is that certain risks — falling ill, growing too old to work, losing a job, being born into poverty — are faced by almost everyone at some point and are too large for individuals to bear alone, so society should pool them. In practice this usually rests on a few pillars: pensions for the elderly, healthcare, support for the unemployed and disabled, and publicly funded education.
extra_html: Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the welfare state's growth across the 20th century, especially after the Great Depression and the Second World War, as governments expanded their role from keeping order to actively safeguarding living standards. Countries differ widely in how generous and comprehensive their systems are, producing distinct "models" of welfare. What they share is the basic idea of a social safety net — a floor below which citizens are not supposed to fall. The welfare state is also one of the most persistent subjects of political debate, and the debate maps closely onto the left-right spectrum. Supporters argue it reduces poverty and inequality, stabilizes the economy, and gives people security to take risks; critics worry about its cost and the taxes needed to fund it, its effects on economic growth and work incentives, and the proper balance between collective provision and individual responsibility. Few argue for abolishing it entirely; the live question in most democracies is how large, how generous, and how designed it should be.

related.title: Taxation & Public Budgets
related.hook: A government's budget is its values written in numbers — and taxation is how it raises the money to act at all. Follow the money to understand the priorities.

related.title: Public Goods & the State
related.hook: Some things markets struggle to provide — clean air, national defense, street lighting — because no one can be charged for them. That gap is a core reason states exist.

related.title: Markets, Regulation & the Mixed Economy
related.hook: Pure free market or full state control? Almost every country picks neither — they run a mixed economy, and where they draw the line is one of politics' great arguments.

related.title: Global Inequality & Development
related.hook: Where you're born still shapes your life chances more than almost anything else. Closing that gap between rich and poor nations is one of politics' great unfinished projects.

flashcards.back_html: Government provision for citizens' basic economic security and well-being — typically pensions, healthcare, unemployment support, and education.

flashcards.prompt: What is the central aim of the welfare state?

choices.text: To cushion people against risks like illness, old age, and joblessness
To guarantee everyone the same income exactly

flashcards.explanation_html: The welfare state pools risk so that misfortune like sickness or unemployment doesn't leave people destitute.

flashcards.prompt: What do debates about the welfare state mainly concern?

choices.text: Its size, cost, and effects on the economy and individual responsibility
The wording of the national anthem

flashcards.explanation_html: Disagreement focuses on how large and generous it should be and its trade-offs, not usually on abolishing it altogether.
